test.title: An island that makes its own power

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the island of Keldon depended on a single cable from the mainland for its electricity. When storms damaged the cable, as they did several times a decade, the island’s 400 residents could be without power for days.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: In 2012 a community group proposed building three wind turbines and owning them jointly. Banks were reluctant to lend money to a group with no experience, so the project was paid for partly by a government grant and partly by residents, who bought shares for as little as £50 each.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The turbines now produce more electricity than the island uses. The surplus is sold to the mainland through the same cable that once brought power in, and the income, around £120,000 in a good year, is shared between the shareholders and a fund for local projects.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The fund has paid for insulation in older houses, a new roof for the village hall and an electric minibus that takes elderly residents to the doctor. Not all islanders were enthusiastic at first: some objected to the noise and the view, and two turbines were moved further from homes after complaints.
paragraphs.label: D
